meta.description: Genuine Che Guevara, from Socialism and Man in Cuba (Marcha, 12 March 1965). The standard translation says "great feelings of love," plural.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'At the risk of seeming ridiculous, let me say that the true revolutionary is guided by a great feeling of love'?
meta.ogDescription: Che Guevara wrote it in Socialism and Man in Cuba (1965). The Spanish says "grandes sentimientos de amor": great feelings, plural, not a great feeling.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1928–1967 · Argentine-born revolutionary, a leader of the Cuban Revolution
answer.sourceLine: From Guevara’s essay-letter Socialism and Man in Cuba, published in the Montevideo weekly Marcha on 12 March 1965. Checked against the Spanish original and the Ocean Press English translation, which reads “great feelings of love.” The popular singular “a great feeling of love” is a one-word drift.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Socialism and Man in Cuba (El socialismo y el hombre en Cuba)
Marcha (Montevideo), 12 March 1965, as “From Algiers, for Marcha. The Cuban Revolution Today”
Spanish: “Déjeme decirle, a riesgo de parecer ridículo, que el revolucionario verdadero está guiado por grandes sentimientos de amor.”
Ocean Press, as given on marxists.org (credited to The Che Reader, © 2005)

source.excerpt: At the risk of seeming ridiculous, let me say that the true revolutionary is guided by great feelings of love. It is impossible to think of a genuine revolutionary lacking this quality. Perhaps it is one of the great dramas of the leader that he or she must combine a passionate spirit with a cold intelligence and make painful decisions without flinching.
trail: The Spanish original, El socialismo y el hombre en Cuba ↗, has “Déjeme decirle, a riesgo de parecer ridículo, que el revolucionario verdadero está guiado por grandes sentimientos de amor.” A note on the page says Carlos Quijano published the letter in Marcha on 12 March 1965.

The Ocean Press translation on marxists.org ↗ reads “At the risk of seeming ridiculous, let me say that the true revolutionary is guided by great feelings of love.” That is the popular wording except for the plural.
An alternate translation by Margarita Zimmermann ↗ renders the same sentence as “Let me say, with the risk of appearing ridiculous, that the true revolutionary is guided by strong feelings of love.”
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line under “Man and Socialism in Cuba (1965)” with the singular “a great feeling of love,” while linking the Ocean Press text, which says “feelings.”
source.excerptNote: The popular version changes “great feelings of love” to “a great feeling of love.” The Spanish has the plural, “grandes sentimientos de amor.” The surrounding passage is about what the revolution costs its leaders.

author.heading: About Che Guevara
author.metaLine: 1928–1967 · Argentine-born Marxist revolutionary, a leader of the Cuban Revolution
author.bio: Ernesto “Che” Guevara was an Argentine-born doctor who became a guerrilla commander in the Cuban Revolution and then held senior posts in Fidel Castro’s government. His 1965 essay Socialism and Man in Cuba sets out his idea of the “new man” that socialism was supposed to create. He was killed in Bolivia in October 1967.

misattribution.heading: Right author, slightly wrong words
misattribution.intro: Unlike many lines pinned on Guevara, this one is genuine. What drifts is the English: there are several translations, and the most-shared version doesn’t match any of the ones checked here word for word.

items.who: “guided by a great feeling of love”
items.why: The Ocean Press translation ↗ says “great feelings of love,” and the Spanish ↗ has the plural “grandes sentimientos de amor.” The singular turns up in retellings, including Wikiquote ↗.

The Margarita Zimmermann translation ↗ opens “Let me say, with the risk of appearing ridiculous…” and uses “strong feelings of love.” It is the same sentence, translated differently, not a different quote.

misattribution.truthLine: Guevara wrote it in Socialism and Man in Cuba (Marcha, 12 March 1965): “Déjeme decirle, a riesgo de parecer ridículo, que el revolucionario verdadero está guiado por grandes sentimientos de amor” (Spanish text ↗).

context.heading: Why the line is remembered
lead: The sentence comes from a long letter to Carlos Quijano, editor of the Uruguayan weekly Marcha. In it, Guevara argues that socialism must create a “new man.” The love passage sits in his account of the revolutionary vanguard. He says a leader must “combine a passionate spirit with a cold intelligence and make painful decisions without flinching,” and that leaders give up ordinary family life to the revolution.

That pairing of love with cold, painful decisions is why the line keeps being argued over. A UMass open textbook ↗ sets it against the Cuban revolutionaries’ public executions and asks students to explain the phrase “great feelings of love.”
